tldr: This paper proposes "sLoTh," a continual learning framework for energy-efficient spiking Vision Transformers that adapts sequentially by updating less than 1% of parameters without storing past data. It maintains high accuracy even as the number of tasks grows, while cutting energy consumption by about 6.5x compared to conventional dense ViTs.
hero_caption: A comparison diagram of three continual learning paradigms (TIL, CIL, and OCL). It outlines the differences between TIL (where task IDs are provided during inference), CIL (which identifies all known classes without task IDs), and OCL (the most challenging streaming setting with a single data pass and no task boundaries).
overview:
For robots and edge devices to operate autonomously in dynamic environments, continual learning—adapting to incoming new data without forgetting previously acquired knowledge—is essential. However, existing Vision Transformers (ViTs) rely on dense computation, consuming too much energy to fit within robotic battery and resource limits. On the other hand, while event-driven, energy-efficient Spiking Neural Network (SNN)-based Transformers have attracted attention, efficient continual learning using pretrained models has remained largely unexplored.

To address this, the authors developed "sLoTh," a continual learning framework for pretrained sparse event-based Transformers. Keeping the backbone weights frozen, it restricts plasticity to two components: a lightweight, task-shared scalable-efficient low-rank attention adaptation (seLoRA) and a biologically inspired neuronal firing threshold offset adjustment (threshold modulation). In addition, it incorporates a multi-objective distillation and regularization mechanism without saving any past image data (rehearsal-free).

Evaluations on benchmarks such as CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that sLoTh updates less than 1% of total model parameters while achieving roughly 6.5x lower energy consumption compared to conventional dense ViTs. In challenging class-incremental settings with many fine-grained splits (20 or 50 tasks) as well as online continual learning without task boundaries, it matched or outperformed existing methods that store large amounts of past data in memory buffers.
contributions: Conducted the first systematic study of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for continual learning in pretrained sparse event-based (spiking) Vision Transformers.
Proposed the "sLoTh" framework, combining shared seLoRA and channel-wise threshold modulation without requiring replay buffers to store past data or task-specific architectural expansion.
Achieved approximately 6.5x lower energy consumption compared to conventional ViT-based continual learning while updating less than 1% of model parameters.

Demonstrated superior performance over replay-based methods in challenging online continual learning (OCL) with single-pass data and no task boundaries, thanks to an adaptive snapshot mechanism triggered by loss spikes.

sections.heading: Toward Energy-Friendly Continual Learning for Edge Robotics
sections.summary: Continual learning is essential for robots adapting to dynamic environments, but conventional ViTs suffer from heavy computational cost and high power consumption. This section introduces the overview and contributions of "sLoTh," a new approach combining energy-efficient event-driven Transformers and parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) for sequential learning without storing past data.
sections.details:
Even deep learning models that excel on large static datasets suffer from catastrophic forgetting when data arrives sequentially, overwriting past knowledge when learning new tasks. Recent trends have shifted from CNNs to pretrained ViTs, but naive fine-tuning of ViTs triggers severe forgetting and incurs massive computational overhead. While PEFT techniques (such as LoRA and adapters) that update only a fraction of parameters have emerged as effective solutions, they target artificial neural networks (ANNs) and leave the energy issue of dense attention computation unaddressed.

This highlights the appeal of Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), which perform computation only when spikes (events) occur, much like biological brains. While sparse event-based Transformers such as Spikformer offer high energy efficiency, how to enable continual learning on pretrained models—especially in rehearsal-free settings that store no past data—remained largely unexplored.

To tackle this challenge, this paper introduces sLoTh. By freezing the backbone and combining shared low-rank attention adaptation (seLoRA), neuronal firing threshold modulation, and multi-objective distillation regularization, it enables sequential adaptation updating less than 1% of parameters without model expansion or replay buffers.

captions.F1: A diagram illustrating three continual learning paradigms. Difficulty increases toward the bottom right: TIL provides task boundaries and task IDs at test time; CIL identifies all classes without task IDs; and OCL streams data in a single pass without task boundaries.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Continual Learning, PEFT, and Spiking Networks
sections.summary: This section reviews existing continual learning approaches (regularization, rehearsal, and architectural expansion) alongside PEFT trends for Transformers. It positions the work by noting that most SNN continual learning studies focus on CNN backbones or training from scratch, leaving PEFT for pretrained event-based Transformers unexplored.
sections.details:
Existing approaches to continual learning broadly fall into three categories:
- Regularization-based: Penalizes parameter updates based on importance metrics (e.g., EWC, Synaptic Intelligence). These are memory-efficient, but often struggle to preserve accuracy in large-scale settings.
- Rehearsal-based: Stores past samples in a buffer to replay during training (e.g., Experience Replay, DER). While dominant in online continual learning (OCL), storing raw data raises privacy concerns and is difficult under edge memory constraints.
- Architecture-based: Allocates or expands dedicated modules for each task. The downside is that parameter count grows unbounded as tasks accumulate.

Meanwhile, PEFT methods for pretrained ViTs (prompt tuning like L2P, adapters, LoRA variants) are actively researched, but they all assume dense-computation ANNs.

In the SNN domain, event-driven, energy-efficient models like Spikformer and QKFormer have emerged, but continual learning applications have primarily relied on CNN backbones or buffer-based rehearsal. This paper represents the first systematic attempt at rehearsal-free PEFT continual learning for pretrained event-driven Transformers.

sections.heading: How sLoTh Works: Threshold Modulation, seLoRA, and Autonomous Detection
sections.summary: sLoTh freezes the backbone and updates only channel-wise firing threshold offsets and a task-shared low-rank attention module (seLoRA). It also introduces distillation and anchor losses to preserve past knowledge, along with a loss-spike trigger that acts as pseudo-task boundaries during online learning.
sections.details:
The core design philosophy of sLoTh is to "preserve the geometric structure of the backbone and grant minimal, well-targeted plasticity."

### 3.1 Problem Setting
The model sequentially learns a series of tasks with disjoint class sets. The paper addresses class-incremental learning (CIL) and task-incremental learning (TIL) where task IDs are not provided at test time, as well as online continual learning (OCL) where data streams in a single pass.

### 3.2 Model Plasticity (Trainable Modules)
- Channel-wise Excitability Modulation: Inspired by neuromodulatory gain control in biological brains, it adds a learnable offset $\delta_c$ per feature channel to the base threshold $v_{\text{th}}^{\text{base}}$. Because connection weights remain untouched, distortion of the feature space is minimal, pairing exceptionally well with prototype-based classifiers.
- Scalable-Efficient LoRA (seLoRA): Introduces low-rank matrices $A, B$ into attention projection matrices. Unlike existing methods that instantiate new LoRA modules for every task, sLoTh maintains a single shared module, preventing parameter growth regardless of task count.

### 3.3 Learning Losses for Stabilization
In addition to the cross-entropy loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}$ on the current task, stabilization terms are applied: a teacher-student logit distillation loss to preserve historical output distributions, a Local Anchor preventing sudden parameter drift from the immediate prior snapshot, and a Global Anchor preventing excessive divergence from initialization.

### 3.4 & 3.5 Classifier and Online Novelty Detection
During training, a cosine classifier is used, updating only new class weights at task completion. At inference, nearest class mean (NCM) classification using feature prototypes is employed to avoid recency bias. For OCL without explicit boundaries, a lightweight trigger monitors the ratio of current loss to its running average; exceeding a threshold $\gamma$ flags a distribution shift (new classes appearing) and updates the teacher snapshot autonomously.

sections.heading: Empirical Results: 6.5x More Energy Efficient, Excelling on Fine-Grained Tasks
sections.summary: Using QKFormer as the primary backbone, sLoTh was evaluated on CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, Tiny-ImageNet, and others. It achieved roughly 6.5x lower energy consumption than standard ViTs and outperformed existing PEFT methods as task splits became finer (20 to 100 tasks).
sections.details:
Experiments primarily utilized a pretrained QKFormer (64M parameters), evaluated on Average Accuracy (AA) and Average Forgetting (F).

### 4.1 & 4.2 Class-Incremental Learning (CIL) Results
On CIFAR-100 with a coarse 10-task split, ViT-based methods like SD-LoRA held an initial lead (88.01%), but degraded sharply as splits grew to 20 and 50 tasks. In contrast, Full sLoTh reached 84.65% across 20 tasks and 87.22% across 50 tasks, outperforming all baselines. A similar pattern appeared on ImageNet-R: while achieving 71.61% at $T=5$, it rose to a benchmark-best 77.10% at $T=20$. Spiking dynamics paired with lightweight adaptation prove robust during prolonged sequential updates.

### 4.3 Remarkable Resilience in Online Continual Learning (OCL)
In single-pass, boundary-free OCL, sLoTh was compared against strong replay methods (e.g., MOE-MOSE) storing 5,000 to 10,000 past samples. The completely buffer-free Full sLoTh scored 55.12% (forgetting 12.79) on CIFAR-100, closely matching buffered MOE-MOSE (55.62%). On 100-task Tiny-ImageNet, Full sLoTh achieved 42.90%, outperforming MOE-MOSE (38.41%) by roughly 4.5 percentage points.

### 4.4 & 4.5 Plasticity Trade-offs and Loss Ablations
While Full sLoTh combining seLoRA and threshold modulation excelled in multi-epoch CIL (81.23%), single-pass OCL revealed an interesting dynamic: simpler parameter updates such as seLoRA-only (63.88%) or threshold-only (60.25%) achieved higher performance during fast adaptation. In loss ablations, removing KL distillation dropped accuracy from 55.12% down to 10.23%, verifying that anchor and distillation terms are vital for mitigating forgetting.

sections.heading: Summary: New Horizons for Edge AI Inspired by Biology
sections.summary: sLoTh proves that a rehearsal-free framework storing zero past data can match or exceed replay-based methods while operating at a fraction of the energy. Combining bio-inspired threshold control with structured attention adaptation provides a compelling blueprint for continual edge learning.
sections.details:
The key achievement of this work is demonstrating that in severe online continual learning—where past data storage (replay buffers) was long considered indispensable—leveraging intrinsic properties of spiking neural networks (firing threshold modulation) can achieve competitive accuracy without any buffer.

Modulating neuronal excitability without altering synaptic weights is fundamentally effective at preventing catastrophic representation drift. Because memory consumption does not scale with task count, it is uniquely suited for physical robots and edge devices facing strict memory and power constraints.

Furthermore, the findings reveal that CIL and OCL favor different plasticity dynamics: multi-epoch regimes benefit from combined plasticity mechanisms, whereas single-pass streaming regimes respond faster to simpler, less constrained adaptation. This provides valuable design guidance for future architectures.

sections.heading: Appendix: Algorithmic Details and Preliminary PEFT Validations
sections.summary: The appendix details exact mathematical formulations of the loss terms, algorithmic steps for OCL, and preliminary ablation experiments evaluating which PEFT adapters work best on QKFormer.
sections.details:
- Preliminary PEFT Comparison (Table 9): Testing various PEFT setups on QKFormer showed that inserting standard adapters achieved 87.21% accuracy, but parameter accumulation per task was prohibitive. Threshold modulation alone reached 70.56% while requiring over 10x fewer updated parameters than LoRA (80.89%), demonstrating extreme parameter efficiency.
- Detailed Loss Formulations: Parameter drift is constrained via three regularizers: logit distillation against the prior task snapshot, a local anchor $\mathcal{L}_{\text{local}} = \|\psi - \psi_{\text{local}}\|^2$, and a global anchor $\mathcal{L}_{\text{global}} = \|\psi - \psi_0\|^2$.
- Novelty Detection Behavior: The trigger evaluates the ratio of current batch loss to its running average, $r_b = \mathcal{L}_b / \bar{\mathcal{L}}_b$. Exceeding threshold $\gamma$ indicates a pseudo-task boundary, prompting a teacher snapshot update. A threshold set too low causes false positives and extra computation, whereas a threshold set too high delays adaptation.

takeaways: Using SNN-based Transformers (e.g., QKFormer) instead of dense ViTs for continual learning reduces energy consumption by about 6.5x while preserving competitive accuracy.
Neuronal firing threshold offset modulation, inspired by biological neuromodulation, preserves learned representations without modifying synaptic weights, effectively curbing catastrophic forgetting.
Employing a single task-shared LoRA alongside multi-objective distillation anchors prevents parameter explosion regardless of how many tasks are added.
Multi-epoch CIL and single-pass OCL require distinct plasticity dynamics; simpler adaptation modules perform better during fast, single-pass streaming adaptation.
limitations: Novelty detection in OCL relies on a simple threshold on loss spikes, which can be sensitive to noise or sudden difficulty variations, leading to false detections or delayed updates.
In coarse, few-task initial stages, accuracy remains a few percentage points behind conventional dense ViT PEFT methods such as SD-LoRA.
The approach has not yet been validated with physical neuromorphic hardware implementations or deployed on real-time sensor streams in physical robot environments.
